hints: Think about what happens to the kinetic energy of a fast electron when it passes close to a positive nucleus in the target - does it keep all its speed or lose some?
Consider whether every electron loses exactly the same amount of energy in one hit, or if there are many possible amounts of energy loss.
Link the energy lost by an electron in a single interaction to the energy, and so frequency, of the single photon that is created.
walkthrough:
**What produces the X-rays - braking radiation**
Think of the fast electrons crashing into the metal. As an electron passes near a positively charged nucleus it is attracted and sharply slowed down, or decelerated. The kinetic energy it loses does not disappear, it is emitted as a single X-ray photon. This is called bremsstrahlung or braking radiation.

**Why not all the same energy**
Not every electron has the same close encounter. Some pass very close and stop almost completely, some are only slightly deflected, and many suffer multiple smaller collisions. So there is a whole range of possible decelerations and a whole range of possible energy losses.

**From energy loss to continuous spectrum**
For one interaction: $$E_{photon} = \text{energy lost by electron}$$ A large deceleration gives a high-energy photon, a small deceleration gives a low-energy photon. Because the deceleration can take any value up to a maximum, the photon energy takes any value up to a maximum, which is a continuous spectrum.

Final answer: Incident electrons are decelerated by the target nuclei and lose kinetic energy as X-ray photons (bremsstrahlung). Different electrons undergo different amounts of deceleration, so different amounts of energy are lost. Photon energy equals energy lost, giving a continuous range of photon energies.

hints: Start by thinking when the photon energy is largest - what must happen to the full 15 keV of kinetic energy gained by an electron?
Recall how to connect electron kinetic energy from the accelerating voltage to photon energy from its wavelength using $eV$ and $hc/\lambda$.
walkthrough:
**Highest energy means full energy in one photon**
An electron accelerated through $V = 15 \text{ kV}$ gains kinetic energy: $$E_{max} = eV$$ The most energetic X-ray is made when one electron gives all of this energy to a single photon in one violent stop. So: $$E_{photon,max} = eV = \frac{hc}{\lambda_{min}}$$

**Rearrange for minimum wavelength**
Highest energy means smallest wavelength, since $E = hc/\lambda$. Rearranging: $$\lambda_{min} = \frac{hc}{eV}$$

**Put in numbers**
$$V = 15000 \text{ V}$$ $$\lambda_{min} = \frac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3.0 \times 10^{8})}{(1.60 \times 10^{-19})(15000)}$$ $$\lambda_{min} = \frac{1.989 \times 10^{-25}}{2.40 \times 10^{-15}} \approx 8.3 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}$$ This is the short-wavelength limit of the continuous spectrum.
Final answer: Maximum photon energy = $eV = hc/\lambda_{min}$. $\lambda_{min} = hc/(eV) = 8.3 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}$.

hints: Recall the linearised form of the attenuation law - what does a graph of $\ln(I/I_{o})$ against $x$ look like and what is its gradient in terms of $\mu$?
Pick two widely spaced, easy-to-read points on the straight line in Fig. 11.1 to find rise over run and so $\mu$ with unit $\text{cm}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
**Linearise the exponential**
Intensity falls exponentially: $$I = I_{o}e^{-\mu x}$$ Taking natural logs: $$\ln\left(\frac{I}{I_{o}}\right) = -\mu x$$ So a plot of $\ln(I/I_{o})$ against $x$ is a straight line through the origin with gradient $= -\mu$.

**Find the gradient from Fig. 11.1**
Read off the line. For example at $x = 10.0 \text{ cm}$, $\ln(I/I_{o}) \approx -2.08$. Then: $$\mu = -\frac{\Delta \ln(I/I_{o})}{\Delta x} = -\frac{-2.08 - 0}{10.0 - 0}$$ $$\mu \approx 0.21 \text{ cm}^{-1}$$ Any large triangle gives $0.20$ to $0.22 \text{ cm}^{-1}$.
Final answer: $\ln(I/I_{o}) = -\mu x$, so $\mu = -$ gradient. Gradient $\approx -0.21$, giving $\mu \approx 0.21 \text{ cm}^{-1}$.

hints: Translate 5.0% of initial intensity into a value for the ratio $I/I_{o}$ and then for $\ln(I/I_{o})$.
Use your value of $\mu$ from (b)(i) in $\ln(I/I_{o}) = -\mu x$ and solve for the thickness $x$.
walkthrough:
**Set up the required fraction**
Reduced to 5.0% means: $$\frac{I}{I_{o}} = 0.050$$ Insert into the attenuation law: $$\ln(0.050) = -\mu x$$ where $\ln(0.050) \approx -3.00$.

**Solve for thickness**
Using $\mu \approx 0.21 \text{ cm}^{-1}$: $$x = \frac{-\ln(0.050)}{\mu} = \frac{3.00}{0.21}$$ $$x \approx 14 \text{ cm}$$ A thicker layer is needed because tissue is not very absorbing for this beam.
